newsitem.title: UK: UK's Britannia says mutual loyalty bonus pays off.
newsitem.headline: UK's Britannia says mutual loyalty bonus pays off.

text.p: The chief executive of Britain's Britannia Building Society said on Thursday the company was reaping the rewards of its loyalty scheme.
"We've been delighted with the response," John Heaps said in an interview on the final day of the Building Societies Association (BSA) annual meeting.

Britannia's loyalty bonus scheme was launched a year ago. The mutually-owned society's savers and borrowers earn points depending on the length and depth of their relationship with the group. At the end of the year these are converted into cash.

Heaps said the average pay-out had been around 35 pounds, while the highest amount paid out had been around 500 pounds. The Britannia, which has 1.8 million members, paid out a total of 35 million pounds.

The scheme was devised as a way of countering the move to stock exchange flotation pursued by other building societies, including Britain's biggest homelender Halifax, which is due to be listed on June 1.

Once the current round of conversions, which includes Woolwich and Northern Rock, is over, Britannia will rank third among the remaining building societies with total assets of just over 16.0 billion pounds at the end of 1996.

Other societies have adjusted their savings and loans rates to underline the benefits to members of staying mutual rather than opting for a one-off windfall in the form of shares in the converting societies.
Heaps said pursuing the loyalty route had taken some bravery on the part of Britannia as it had not been an easy thing to set up, with start-up costs of some six million pounds.

He said the scheme was about "retention and cross sales" and keeping people, giving Britannia a valuable database on their customers and the facility to sell them other products such as personal equity plans (PEPs) and life insurance.

But he conceded that changing rates to make them more competitive than bank rivals was an easier road to follow in the short term and he was not surprised that this had been adopted by other societies.

Making a distribution to members was, said Heaps, not only proving extremely popular with Britannia's members but also imposed a discipline on the society's management which altering rates would not have done.

"It starts to put some accountability disciplines on our board," Heaps said, pointing out that members would expect the bonus to rise or at least not to fall below previous levels in much the same way as shareholders do with a dividend in publicly-owned companies.
Britannia was not considering merging with other building societies but will continue to look to buy mortgage books.
Other building societies would reconsider their own strategies and smaller ones could merge because of factors hindering their development of competitive mortgage pricing.

The need for sophisticated treasury techniques, access to retail deposits and the cost pressures of investment in information technology were all factors which could spur further merger activity in the sector.

Heaps was upbeat about the prospects for the mutual sector, which he said had gathered a head of steam since last year when a number of the larger societies announced they would convert and become banks.
"They have got a big role to play going forward," he said.
